pages.text: Lawrence sat in the back of his father’s car, stuck in traffic again. Beside the road, a concrete-lined drain ran black with rubbish. “Dad,” he said, “what if we could get rid of the drain and the traffic?” His father, an engineer, laughed. “You are not the first to dream of that,” he said. “In Seoul, in Korea, they actually did something like it.”

pages.alt: A boy looks from a car window at a black, rubbish-filled drain beside a jammed road.

pages.text: At school, Madam Fosu showed the class a map of Seoul. “Long ago,” she said, “a stream called the Cheonggyecheon ran through the city centre. As the city grew, people dumped waste into it, and it became dirty. In the late 1950s, the stream was covered with concrete, and in the years that followed, a six-lane elevated highway was built on top. By 1971 it was the main road of the city.”

“Long ago,” she said, “a stream called the Cheonggyecheon ran through the city centre.
As the city grew, people dumped waste into it, and it became dirty.
In the late 1950s, the stream was covered with concrete, and in the years that followed, a six-lane elevated highway was built on top.
By 1971 it was the main road of the city.”
pages.alt: A teacher shows a map and a drawing of a highway built over a buried stream.

pages.text: “But decades later,” she continued, “the city made a bold decision. In 2003, the highway began to be demolished. Construction on the stream began in 2004, and the restored stream opened in October 2005. The new stream is about six kilometres long, with bridges and footpaths on both sides.” Lawrence leaned forward. “They destroyed the road?” he asked. “They did,” said Madam Fosu.

pages.alt: Workers use machines to break up a concrete highway as a city watches.

pages.text: “It was not easy,” she said. “Many shopkeepers feared that they would lose customers, and drivers feared worse traffic. The project cost about US$380 million. And I must be honest: the water in the new stream is not all natural. It is brought in from the Han River and from groundwater collected at underground stations.” A girl raised her hand. “Then was it worth it?” she asked. “That is what you must decide,” said Madam Fosu.

pages.text: “Here are some reports,” she said. “The stream has become a popular green space, and visitors number in the tens of thousands each day. Studies report that the area is cooler than nearby streets, by as much as five degrees, and that air pollution has fallen. Dozens of plant, fish and bird species have been recorded. Many people say it has brought nature back into the heart of the city.” Lawrence began to draw.

pages.text: That evening, Lawrence told his father about the lesson. “Accra has many buried drains,” said Mr Adomako. “But it is not as simple as lifting a lid. Every city has its own floods, its own traffic and its own money. Seoul had a plan, a budget, strong leaders and years of work.” He ruffled his son’s hair. “Maybe you will be the engineer who makes a plan like that for us.” Lawrence smiled. “Maybe,” he said.

pages.text: For homework, Madam Fosu asked the class to write a descriptive paragraph about a place. Lawrence wrote: “The stream glided softly between stone banks, and the cool air carried the smell of wet leaves. Children’s laughter echoed from the bridges while willow branches brushed the water. Overhead, the traffic hummed like a distant beehive, but here, beside the water, the city felt calm.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a descriptive paragraph uses the five senses: sight, sound, smell, touch and taste. Lawrence used sight (“stone banks”), smell (“wet leaves”) and sound (“laughter echoed”), and a comparison (“like a distant beehive”). He wrote in one tense, the past. Use strong, exact words, and never a chat shortcut. The end.
